statement: A jar holds 45 beads. Some are red, some are blue, and 9 are green. There are as many red beads as blue beads. How many red beads are there?

choices.misconception: I took away the 9 green beads and then shared the other 36 among three colours instead of two.
I shared all 45 beads equally among the three colours, as if there were as many green beads as red.
I found the 18 red beads and then added the 9 green beads to them.
I took away the 9 green beads and stopped, forgetting to split the rest between red and blue.

hints: Which beads are not red or blue?
Draw a bar for the whole jar. Cut off the green part, then split what is left into two equal parts, one red and one blue.
Without the green beads there are $45 - 9 = 36$ beads, shared equally between red and blue.

solutions.reliable: Take away the green beads: $45 - 9 = 36$ beads are red or blue. Red and blue are equal, so each is $36 \div 2 = 18$. Check: $18 + 18 + 9 = 45$. The transferable idea: remove the part you know, then split what is left into equal parts.

whyOnTest: A part-whole bar model: remove the known part first, then split the rest into equal parts.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
